title: At work: careers
subtitle: cold calling, niche market, red tape, hammer out a deal
summary: Talk about sales and business careers in advanced English - the hard sell, purchasing power, loss leaders, takeovers and the red tape in between.

lesson.heading: A career in sales
lesson.text: **Telesales** and **telemarketing** both mean selling or marketing goods and services by phone. **Cold calling** is phoning people who have not requested a call in order to try to sell them something, and the **hard sell** is an attempt to sell by being very forceful or persuasive.

examples.text: When Carl left school, he took the first job he was offered - in **telesales**.
Most of the people he phoned hated **cold calling** and put the phone down when he tried the **hard sell**.
He became quite skilled at persuading customers to **part with their money**.

lesson.heading: Moving up in sales
lesson.text: A **shopping channel** is a TV channel devoted to selling products, and **merchandise** means products that are bought and sold. If you have **never looked back** since a decision, you have moved forward successfully ever since.

examples.text: He moved into a job on a TV **shopping channel**, where he specialised in selling **merchandise** for the leisure market.
The shops are hoping to sell a lot of **merchandise** connected with the royal wedding.
Helga has never **looked back** since she started her own business ten years ago.

lesson.heading: Buying and shopping
lesson.text: A person's **purchasing power** is the amount of money they have available to buy goods. If you **shop around**, you try different shops to see which offers best value. A shop **stocks** an item if it keeps a supply of it - it **keeps it in stock**.

examples.text: It's a sensible idea to **shop around** a bit before buying a computer.
The shop I went to didn't **stock** the printer I wanted so I'm going to order it online.
People sometimes make a purchasing decision based on **brand loyalty**.
examples.note: brand loyalty = confidence in a particular make and a tendency always to choose it

lesson.heading: Selling strategies
rows: buy something, usually a car or house, of higher value than the one you had
buy something cheaper than the one you had
an item sold below cost to attract people into the shop
a specialised group of customers with particular interests
be sold at an auction, to the highest bidder

lesson.heading: Auctions and markets
lesson.text: At an **auction** people make gradually increasing **bids** and the item is sold to the highest bidder; we say it **goes under the hammer**. A company that finds a **niche market** has found a specialised group of customers whose particular needs it can meet.

examples.text: A world-famous painting will go **under the hammer** in London tomorrow.
I'm going to make a **bid** for the dining table that is up for auction tomorrow.
They produce special clothes for people who practise yoga and have really cornered this **niche market**.
I think those new games consoles are **priced** too high at the moment.

lesson.heading: A career in business
lesson.text: A **lucrative** business produces a lot of money. **Red tape** is bureaucracy (a negative word), and **administration** is the organisation and arrangement of operations. A **proposition** is a formal offer; a **takeover** is an agreement in which one company takes control of another, while in a **merger** two companies join together to become one.

examples.text: Sportswear is a very **lucrative** business to be in at the moment.
There's a lot of **red tape** involved in setting up a new business.
Hassan has made a rather interesting **proposition** about setting up a business together.
At the moment they are discussing **a takeover** of another company.

lesson.heading: Doing the deal
lesson.text: When two sides **reach a compromise**, both reduce their demands a little; when they **hammer out a deal**, they talk in detail until a business agreement is made. A company that has been **swallowed up** has been taken over by a larger one. **Capital assets** are the buildings and machines a company owns, and money can be used to **invest in** a business **start-up**.

examples.text: They managed to **reach a compromise** and **hammer out a deal** without too much delay.
A number of small companies have been **swallowed up** by that huge multinational.
She used the money raised by the sale of her **capital assets** to **invest in** a business **start-up**.
Banks will only lend a **start-up** money if it has a realistic business plan.

lesson.text: You reach a compromise and hammer out a deal - the verbs are fixed. Trade up means buy something dearer, trade down something cheaper.

exercises.prompt: Match the two parts of these business collocations.
Match these words to make three more collocations from the unit.
A world-famous painting will go ___ the hammer in London tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: If an item goes or comes under the hammer, it is sold at an auction.

exercises.prompt: It's a sensible idea to shop ___ a bit before buying a computer.
exercises.explanation: To shop around is to try different companies or shops to see which offers best value.

exercises.prompt: Sally set up her own business and she hasn't looked ___ since the day it opened.
exercises.explanation: To never look back means to move forward successfully.

exercises.prompt: I don't mind a hard sell on someone who has expressed an interest, but I hate ___ calling.
exercises.hint: (phoning people who did not ask you to)
exercises.explanation: Cold calling is phoning people who have not requested a call in order to sell them something.

exercises.prompt: It can be quite hard to persuade my dad to ___ with his money.
exercises.explanation: To part with your money is to spend it or give it away.

exercises.prompt: I'm going to make a ___ for the dining table that is up for auction tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: At an auction people make gradually increasing bids and the highest bidder wins.

exercises.prompt: My current job is in ___. I spend all the day on the phone.
exercises.explanation: Telesales and telemarketing both mean selling or marketing goods and services by phone.

exercises.prompt: The shop I went to didn't ___ the printer I wanted so I'm going to order it online.
exercises.explanation: If a shop stocks an item, it keeps a supply of it in stock.

exercises.prompt: As their business interests were quite different, it took them a long time to ___ a deal.
exercises.hint: (talk in detail until an agreement is made)
exercises.explanation: To hammer out a deal is to talk in detail until a business agreement is made.

exercises.prompt: I hope we'll be able to ___ a compromise when we meet tomorrow.
exercises.explanation: You reach a compromise - both sides reduce their demands a little.

exercises.prompt: My sports car was so expensive to run that I decided to trade it ___ for something much cheaper.
exercises.explanation: To trade down is to buy something of lower value; trade up is the opposite.

exercises.prompt: If you want to go into the import and export business, be prepared for a lot of ___.
exercises.explanation: Red tape is bureaucracy - a negative word.

exercises.prompt: A number of small companies have been ___ by that huge multinational in the last six months.
exercises.explanation: To be swallowed up is to be taken over by a larger company.

exercises.statement: In a merger, one company takes control of another one.
exercises.explanation: That is a takeover. In a merger two companies join together to become one company.

exercises.statement: A loss leader is an item sold for less than it costs the shop, to attract customers inside.
exercises.explanation: Correct - once inside, customers also buy more profitable items.

exercises.prompt: Does each term belong to selling to customers, or to running and buying companies?
Put this business sentence in order.
exercises.answer: They managed to reach a compromise and hammer out a deal
exercises.explanation: In a compromise both sides reduce their demands; hammering out a deal is the detailed talking that follows.
